title: What is your plan to not get canceled for AI game dev upon release?
author: AvailableProcess2059
selftext:
Seems the whole world is ready with their pitchforks if you even hint at using AI even though all the big studios are using it behind closed doors.

  
I see three big areas right now for AI:

1 - Coding/development

2 - Art/graphics

3 - Music/SFX

  
Honestly, AI + human retouching is amazing for all three. But seems like a death sentence in the market if you admit or "get caught" on any of these. How do you guys plan to solve this? I'm trying to build a real commercial game and it feels wasteful not to speed it up with the best AI + human workflows.

If your game is good, most people won't care. To give an example, Plains of Pain has like 500 reviews, with very obvious AI-generated character models and dialogue and quest text, and it's sitting at Very Positive.

replies.author: archpawn
replies.body:
The problem with stealing someone's copyrighted work is that it makes it impossible to profit off of it, so there's no incentive to make it. The less your work has to do with the original, the less it matters. AI has basically nothing in common with any individual work it's trained from. It makes it harder for them to profit in the sense that now there's a cheaper and easier way to make nice-looking art, but that's like banning automatic looms because it makes it harder for people who do it by hand to find work.

And when you train those big image models, you're using so much training data that it can't get more than a handful of bytes from each. It doesn't learn anything about any particular image. It just learns what they all have in common. If you are intellectually honest, you can't say that something that tons of images have in common belong to anyone.

It's like with code licenses. Not just because the source code is publicly accessible, that you can include it in your commercial product without respecting the license terms. Sure, there is no supernatural force stopping you, but if you get caught then that will be a problem.

comments.author: ConversationEmpty819
comments.body:
For coding I actually know how to code and have the experience of solo developing and launching a game. I currently do use LLMs but check and improve manually the outputs.
  
For visuals: postprocessing and kit bashing.  
For 2D stuff I have some experience using GIMP, layers filters and most importantly the GMic add-on. I highly recommend checking it, it has a lot of great looking filters that add... Using the luddites term some "soul" to the image. You can even feed the add-on pdf to Gemini and ask it to recommend a workflow for achieving a particular style or mood you'd like. It easily covers the genAI small mistakes and inconsistencies. And that's not even considering that I spend months fine-tuning the AI outputs. Sadly I don't have a strong enough computer to run local models but am getting good results using just the free online services available (Krea, nano banana and Seaart).
  
For 3D I actually love using Blender, but still using genAI for a faster starting. I am currently in the process of developing a method for retopologizing, because I tried many different techniques and don't find any of them fast enough. It's based on mixing different methods I've seen in YouTube and with the help of Gemini. If it works, I'll probably record a YouTube tutorial explaining it because I believe it to be a cool method (basically it implies using the unwrapped UV model for retopologizing, making it 2D and then transform it back into 3D).  
I'm also good at Godot shaders and will use a still perspective and composition effects. That way nobody will recognize the original 3D model as being AIgen after all this process.
  
It's not as fast as "pressing a button and having an asset" like Luddites imply all AIart is, but I'm not focusing on speed that much, I just want to automate the parts that I don't enjoy (drawing and sculpting, boilerplate code, UI) and use manual work for the stuff that I do enjoy (systems code, design, shading, postprocessing).

comments.author: SmoggySPECTEREGaming
comments.body:
Solo Dev here. I am embarking on creating an open world RPG in VR - a very underrepresented VR niche. Having absolutely no coding or game development experience prior. The sheer scope of this project without the help of Ai would be nesr impossible. 

There is a reason it has been 15 years since the last Elder scrolls game and that is with a large budget, team, and creative resources available at their disposal. I have none of those things. My team is my AI copilots - those who coach me to code, the ones who help me come up with story beats that I refine, the music, all of it.

There are a tonne (and I mean  a tonne) of free assets that I have also gotten off the unity asset store + some paid ones that were handcrafted by humans. When people play my game, I want them to be in awe of the scenety, and experience an amazing Game with potentially hundreds of hours of content and get lost in it.

I appreciate posts like this, because I was very worried about the same thing. Just because AI is being used, doesn't mean it needs to feel cheap for the sake of shipping something to make money. If the intention is to build something players will love, then that will shine through. AI is just something to help it cross the finish line. 

In comparison, Call of Duty is handmade or the EA franchise, but with countless MTX, and  new game very year, it feels soulless because its sole intention is to turn a profit.

 It's like any tool, really. In a month, I have accomplished what would easily have taken me years, and it's not even a complete vertical slice yet.
